item.title: HollowByte OpenSSL DoS, NadMesh AI Botnet, and GoldenEyeDog DigiCert Breach
item.content:encoded:
GoldenEyeDog Subgroup Linked to DigiCert Breach and Code-Signing Certificate Theft — Must Read

Researchers attributed DigiCert’s April 2026 breach to CylindricalCanine, a GoldenEyeDog subgroup that compromised support analyst workstations via a malicious “screenshot” file and stole EV code-signing certificate access. The attackers used the certificates to sign Golden Gh0st RAT/Zhong Stealer malware, highlighting the risk of certificate abuse in malware delivery.

  • Expel attributed the April 2026 DigiCert security incident to CylindricalCanine, described as a subgroup of the Chinese cybercrime group GoldenEyeDog, also known as APT-Q-27, Dragon Breath, and Miuuti Group.
  • DigiCert said the threat actor contacted its support team through a customer chat channel on April 2, 2026, and delivered a ZIP file disguised as a customer screenshot that contained a malicious .scr executable.
  • The attackers compromised two DigiCert support analyst workstations and used a customer-support portal function to access initialization codes for approved but pending EV Code Signing certificate orders across a finite set of customer accounts.
  • DigiCert revoked 60 fraudulently obtained certificates, including 27 explicitly linked to the threat actor, and the exploited certificates were used to sign Zhong Stealer malware artifacts.
  • Expel said CylindricalCanine’s attack chain uses phishing files disguised as screenshots, DLL side-loading, and Golden Gh0st RAT, which can steal data, log keystrokes, take screenshots, execute shell commands, and clear Windows Event logs.

New NadMesh Botnet Hunts Exposed AI Services for Cloud Keys and Kubernetes Tokens — Must Read

The new Go-based NadMesh botnet is scanning exposed AI and developer services to steal AWS keys, Kubernetes tokens, Docker credentials, and model/tool access rather than just hijacking compute. Organizations running ComfyUI, Ollama, n8n, Gradio, MCP, Docker, Jenkins, Redis, or similar services should remove them from the public internet, enforce authentication, check persistence paths, and revoke exposed credentials.

  • QiAnXin’s XLab reported that the Go botnet NadMesh appeared in early July and is scanning exposed AI services including ComfyUI, Ollama, n8n, Open WebUI, Langflow, and Gradio.
  • NadMesh collects cloud keys from environment variables, Kubernetes service account tokens, and files such as ~/.aws/config, .env, and ~/.docker/config.json.
  • The operator’s dashboard claimed 3,811 unique AWS keys, while XLab observed distinct source IPs pushing NadMesh rise to about 139 per day in the first week of July.
  • XLab’s observed exploit traffic was led by docker_containers_api_rce at 30.31% and jenkins_scripttext_rce at 22.28%, while mcp_cmd_execute appeared in the smaller unlabeled tail at 0.78%.
  • The article advises operators of exposed services to place them behind authentication or remove them from the public internet, check listed persistence paths, isolate infected hosts, and revoke credentials the host could access.

HollowByte DDoS flaw bloats OpenSSL server memory with 11-byte payload — Should Read

OpenSSL has quietly fixed a DoS flaw called HollowByte that lets unauthenticated attackers bloat server memory using an 11-byte TLS handshake payload. Organizations should update OpenSSL packages to the fixed versions as soon as possible, especially on servers using software like NGINX or Apache.

  • A vulnerability dubbed HollowByte allows unauthenticated attackers to trigger a denial-of-service condition on OpenSSL servers with a malicious payload of just 11 bytes.
  • Vulnerable OpenSSL versions allocate memory based on the declared length in a TLS handshake header before receiving and validating the payload.
  • Okta researchers said repeated connections with randomized claimed sizes can cause heap fragmentation and make a server’s Resident Set Size climb continuously, even after the attacker disconnects.
  • The open-source OpenSSL library is embedded in software including NGINX, Apache web servers, Node.js, Python, Ruby, PHP, MySQL, and PostgreSQL.
  • The issue has been fixed in OpenSSL 4.0.1 and backported to versions 3.6.3, 3.5.7, 3.4.6, and 3.0.21.

Ernst & Young discloses data breach after support system hack — Should Read

Ernst & Young is notifying clients after attackers compromised a third-party support ticket system used by its IT staff and downloaded documents that may contain tax-related personal and financial data. EY says it has removed the unauthorized access and is offering affected clients 24 months of Experian identity monitoring.

  • Ernst & Young is notifying customers of a data breach caused by the compromise of a third-party support ticket system used by its IT personnel.
  • The company determined that an unauthorized third party accessed the platform between March 28 and April 12 and downloaded multiple documents.
  • The affected information included certain personal and financial data contained in or used to prepare tax filings, but the specific data types remain unclear.
  • Ernst & Young has not disclosed how many customers were affected or whether the incident impacts only U.S. customers or customers in other countries as well.
  • EY says it secured its systems, notified federal law enforcement, and is offering affected clients 24 months of identity monitoring and restoration service through Experian.

Inside the Search for "Clean" Residential Proxies for Carding — Optional

Carders increasingly view residential proxies as only one fragile part of a broader fraud stack, prioritizing “clean” IP history, precise location matching, and consistency with device and identity signals. Defenders should not trust residential traffic by itself and should focus on cross-session inconsistencies, velocity, fingerprints, and payment behavior.

  • Flare researchers analyzed 2,889 unique underground posts from the past two years across about 545 discussion threads to study how carders use and evaluate residential proxies.
  • Carders increasingly distinguish between “clean” and “dirty” residential proxy pools based on an IP address’s history and reputation, especially whether it has been used against banks, payment processors, or other fraud-sensitive services.
  • Recent underground discussions describe attempts to match proxy location with stolen identity details such as billing ZIP code, city, time zone, device language, and browser characteristics.
  • The article says residential proxies are frequently combined with antidetect browsers, isolated devices, cookie history, WebRTC configuration, Canvas and WebGL fingerprints, and user-agent consistency.
  • Defenders are advised not to treat residential IP addresses as inherently trustworthy and instead to evaluate consistency across device history, account age, browser fingerprint, payment instrument, billing information, transaction velocity, and post-checkout behavior.

Top Pentera alternatives for automated penetration testing — Optional

Pentera is strong for automated infrastructure and network security validation, but it does not deeply test application and API logic where many fast-moving engineering teams now face the most risk. The article positions Aikido Security as the best alternative for AI-driven application-layer pentesting, while Horizon3 NodeZero is framed as the closest direct alternative for infrastructure-focused testing.

  • Pentera is described as an automated security validation platform focused on infrastructure, internal networks, external attack surfaces, and cloud identity paths, with strengths in Active Directory attack chains, credential abuse, lateral movement, and privilege escalation.
  • The article says Pentera does not deeply test application and API business logic issues such as IDORs, broken access controls, BOLA, or multi-step authenticated workflow flaws.
  • The article argues that application and API testing matters because many organizations deploy significant changes weekly or faster, while only a smaller share validate security on every release.
  • Aikido Security is presented as the strongest alternative for teams needing application and API-layer AI pentesting with autonomous agents, white-box testing, exploit confirmation, and pull requests for fixes.
  • Horizon3 NodeZero is described as the closest direct competitor to Pentera for teams seeking infrastructure and network-focused automated pentesting.

Black Hat Asia 2026: Cleartext Cookie Exposure | Corelight — Optional

Corelight is highlighting cleartext cookie exposure at Black Hat Asia 2026, underscoring the risk of sensitive session data being transmitted or observed without proper protection.

  • The article is titled “Black Hat Asia 2026: Cleartext Cookie Exposure | Corelight.”
  • The article references Black Hat Asia 2026 in its title.
  • The article references cleartext cookie exposure in its title.
  • The article references Corelight in its title.
